docs.title: Arcane Archive – MTG Companion App
docs.text:
Backend API and card-data services for the Arcane Archive mobile application.

Arcane Archive is a Magic: The Gathering(MTG) companion app. It is a user-friendly mobile application that is designed to enhance an MTG player's experience that helps users manage their card collections, create wishlists, build decks, and track their games. In addition to these features, an AI Deck Builder is planned for future implementation.

The backend uses PostgreSQL to persist card data and user information. Scryfall API is integrated to provide card information and images by using the bulk data download feature. An AI-assisted deck builder is planned for future implementation.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Library Management: Provide a card library so users can manage card collections, including library organization, wish lists, card collections, and set management.
  • Card Search: Offer both an advanced and simple user-friendly search feature that allows users to easily find specific cards or sets.
  • Game Tracker: Include essential game tools such as a multi-player game tracker that tracks a player’s name, damage, tax, mana count, counters, life counter, and other game stats.
  • Deck Builder: Provide a comprehensive deck building feature with the ability to save the deck to a user’s library.
  • User Accounts: Support private user accounts, profiles, collections, wishlists, and saved decks.
  • Card Scanner: Provide a card scanner to easily add cards to a user’s library.
  • Mobile Support: Support mobile devices and platforms with user-friendly design.
  • Reliable Card Data: Integrate Scryfall API reference data through controlled API access and bulk data ingestion.

docs.title: Target Audience & Access
docs.text:
Arcane Archive is designed for casual, competitive, and Commander MTG players who want to manage their card collections, build decks, search cards and sets, and track their games. Card browsing and searching are always available for free, but users must create an account to access the full features of the application.

Age Range 8+: The application is designed to be enjoyable for users of all ages, from children to adults. Users under 13 years old must have parental consent and approval to create an account and use the application.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Arcane Archive is a mobile application for Magic: The Gathering players, built with React Native, TypeScript, Expo, and FastAPI. Players can create a profile where their game stats, card library, wish lists, and other preferences are stored. Arcane Archive offers an advanced and simple search feature, a deck builder, user profile, card library, card scanner, and the ability to create wishlists. The app also includes a multi-player game tracker that tracks a player’s name, damage, tax, mana count, counters, a life counter, and other stats. Integrated with Scryfall API, Arcane Archive provides daily updates to the most current card data.

docs.title: Installation and Setup
docs.text: These instructions apply to the backend API. For the mobile app setup information, please refer to the frontend API documentation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Git
  2. Python 3.11 or higher
  3. Poetry for dependency management and virtual environment management
  4. PostgreSQL 15 or higher
  5. Redis
  6. Firebase Account (Optional)
  7. Docker & Docker Compose

docs.title: Install Poetry
docs.text:
Install Poetry using the official installer → Poetry Installation Guide

pip install poetry

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/ARMummert/arcane-archive-backend.git
    cd ./arcane-archive-backend

docs.title: Verify Poetry Version
docs.text:
If you don't have Poetry installed yet, you can install it via the official installer.

poetry --version

docs.title: Create a Poetry Virtual Environment
docs.text:
poetry env activate

poetry env info

This should show you the path to the virtual environment, which should be .venv in the project directory. If it doesn't, you can set it to be in the project directory with:

poetry config virtualenvs.in-project true

source .venv/bin/activate

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text: poetry install

docs.title: Check Docker Configuration
docs.text:
docker --version
docker-compose --version
docker compose config --services

docs.title: Start the Docker Containers
docs.text: docker-compose up -d

docs.title: Environment Configuration
docs.text:
1. Copy the .env.example file into the root directory. 

    cp .env.example .env

  2. Enter your database configuration in the .env file.

DB_USER=Username
DB_PASSWORD=Password
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=arcane_archive_db
  1. Create a separate .env.test file in the test directory for testing purposes.
TEST_DB_USER=Username
TEST_DB_PASSWORD=Password
TEST_DB_HOST=localhost
TEST_DB_PORT=5432
TEST_DB_NAME=arcane_archive_db_test

docs.title: Firebase Configuration
docs.text:
1. Signup or Signin to your Firebase Project and create a Service Account Key.
  2. Configure the provider and mobile-client settings as required by Firebase ADM SDK.
  3. Configure the backend Firebase ADM SDK using firebase_config.py in the config directory.
  4. Save the Service Account Key as service_account.json in the config directory.
  5. Make sure you add the ./config directory to your .gitignore file.
  6. Verify that the backend can validate a Firebase ID token from the correct project.

See the Firebase Authentication Guide and Firebase ADM SDK documentation for more information.

docs.title: Database Migrations
docs.text:
1. Generate the Alembic.ini file in the root directory and edit it to reflect your database configuration.

     poetry run alembic init alembic

  2. Run your database migrations through the Poetry-managed environment.

 poetry run alembic upgrade head
 poetry run alembic current
  1. To create a new migration, run the following command:
 poetry run alembic revision --autogenerate -m "Migration message"
  1. To downgrade the database to a previous migration, run the following command:
 poetry run alembic downgrade <revision>
  1. To view the current revision of the database, run the following command:
 poetry run alembic current

See the Alembic Documentation for more information on Alembic.

docs.title: Initialize Card Data
docs.text:
Run the repositories bulk data ingestion script to download and ingest the Scryfall bulk data into the PostgreSQL database.

poetry run python scripts/ingest_bulk_data.py

docs.title: Launch the API
docs.text:
1. Start the development server. 
 poetry run uvicorn main:app --reload --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000

docs.title: Run Tests
docs.text: poetry run pytest

docs.title: Scryfall API Integration:
docs.text:
To adhere to Scryfall's API usage policies:

  • Daily Updates with ETL Pipeline: Provides daily updates to a full library of MTG cards and sets via ETL Pipeline.
  • Rate Limiting: Request handling with built-in 100 ms rate-limiting
  • Local Storage: Stores card data locally for efficient retrieval and to ensure rate limiting compliance.
  • User Agent: ArcaneArchive/1.0; contact:dev@example.com

docs.text: Endpoint Method Description /cards/search GET Search for cards by name, set, or other criteria /cards/{oracle_id} GET Get card details by Oracle ID /register POST Register a new user /user_accounts GET Get the authenticated user's account details /user_accounts/login POST Authenticate a user and return a token /user_accounts/logout POST Logout the authenticated user and invalidate the token

docs.title: API Access & Rate Limiting
docs.text: Requests to Scryfall API require a user agent string that identifies the application and provides the developer's contact information: ArcaneArchive/1.0; contact: armummert4@gmail.com. It also must include an Accept header. Scryfall enforces a rate limit of 10 requests per second per IP address. To comply with this, Arcane Archive implements a rate-limiter and bounded backoff to protect against too many requests. Bulk exports are preferred over issuing individual API requests.

docs.title: Scryfall's API Usage policies require strict adherence to rate limiting and ethical usage guidelines.
Scryfall API Documentation: https://scryfall.com/docs/api
docs.text: To maintain a healthy relationship with Scryfall and avoid IP bans, the Scryfall Service implements the following constraints:

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Technical Requirements
  • Content and Usage Restrictions
  • Image Usage Restrictions
  • The Arcane Archive Data Contract
  • API Endpoints Overview
  • Legal Disclaimer

docs.title: Technical Requirements
docs.text:
1. User-Agent Header: All requests must include the header: User-Agent: ArcaneArchive/1.0; contact:dev@example.com
  2. Agent Header: All requests must include the header: Agent: ArcaneArchive/1.0

    The Accept header must be present, but you can provide a generic preference. For example, both of these are okay: Accept: / and Accept: application/json;q=0.9,/;q=0.8

  3. HTTPS: All requests must use HTTPS
  4. Rate Limiting: Every outgoing request from the FastAPI backend must be preceded by a minimum 50 – 100 milliseconds of delay between the requests you send to the server at api.scryfall.com
  5. Batching: Arcane Archive uses the /cards/collection endpoint for inventory updates to minimize the total request count.
  6. Data Caching: To minimize requests, you are encouraged to cache data locally for at least 24 hours. Daily bulk data files are available for download for full database access.

Backoff Strategy: In the event of a 429 (Too Many Requests) response, the system implements an Exponential Backoff strategy, pausing all outgoing requests for a specified duration before retrying.

docs.title: Content and Usage Retrictions
docs.text:
When using Scryfall data, you must adhere to the following guidelines:

  • You may not use Scryfall logos or use the Scryfall name in a way that implies Scryfall has endorsed you, your work, or your product.
  • You may not “paywall” access to Scryfall data. You may not require anyone to make payments, take surveys, agree to subscriptions, rate your content, join chat servers, or follow channels in exchange for access to Scryfall data. If you have an account system, end-users should be able to access card data anonymously or with free accounts.
  • You may not use Scryfall data to create new games, or to imply the information and images are from any other game besides Magic: The Gathering.
  • You may not simply repackage, republish, or proxy Scryfall data. Your software must create additional value for end-users.

When using images from Scryfall, you must adhere to the following guidelines:

  • Do not cover, crop, or clip off the copyright or artist name on card images.
  • Do not distort, skew, or stretch card images.
  • Do not blur, sharpen, desaturate, or color-shift card images.
  • Do not add your own watermarks, stamps, or logos to card images.
  • Do not place card images in a way that implies someone other than Wizards of the Coast created the card or that it is from another game besides Magic: The Gathering.
  • When using the art_crop, list the artist name and copyright elsewhere in the same interface presenting the art crop, or use the full card image elsewhere in the same interface. Users should be able to identify the artist and source of the image somehow.

docs.title: Data Engineering and System Design
docs.text:
• To optimize Persistent Storage, we do not store the full Scryfall JSON response.
  • Instead, we perform Data Normalization (for organizing data to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity and consistency) by mapping specific keys to our Pydantic schemas and PostgreSQL tables.
  • To ensure data consistency, we implement Upserts via the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE clause which allows updates without duplicating data.
  • The Scryfall Service (ingestion layer) utilizes an ETL pipeline to map specific Scryfall metadata to our Pydantic schemas and PostgreSQL tables.

docs.title: Data Pipeline Architecture
docs.text:
1. Ingestion Layer: Automated retrieval of Scryfall bulk data via ETL pipeline
  2. Processing Layer: Schema enforcement and normalization using PydanticV2
  3. Persistence Layer: PostgreSQL for reliable and efficient data storage
  4. Orchestration Layer: Scheduled weekly synchronizations to maintain pricing and legality accuracy
flowchart TD
    %% External Data Source
    Scryfall[(Scryfall API / Bulk Data)]

    subgraph Orchestration_Layer [Orchestration Layer]
        Cron[Scheduled Weekly Synchronization]
    end

    subgraph Ingestion_Layer [Ingestion Layer]
        S_Service[Scryfall Service File]
        Stream[Streaming Parser - ijson]
    end

    subgraph Processing_Layer [Processing Layer]
        Pydantic[Pydantic Mapping]
        Normalize[Data Normalization]
    end

    subgraph Persistence_Layer [Persistence Layer]
        Upsert[Atomic Upsert Logic]
        DB[(PostgreSQL Database)]
    end

    %% Flow Connections
    Cron -->|Triggers| S_Service
    Scryfall -.->|Fetch JSON| S_Service
    S_Service --> Stream
    Stream --> Pydantic
    Pydantic --> Normalize
    Normalize --> Upsert
    Upsert --> DB

docs.title: Data Pruning
docs.text:
To maintain data freshness and reduce storage overhead, the Scryfall Service implements a weekly data pruning process. This process removes outdated card data that has not been updated for over a month. The pruning process ensures that the database remains lean and efficient while maintaining the most current card information. 1. Stored Card Attributes:

id, object, name, oracle_id, lang, released_at, image_uris, cmc, mana_cost, keywords, type_line, card_faces, oracle_text, colors, color_identity, color_indicator, legalities, life_modifier, loyalty, power, toughness, foil, nonfoil, set_id, set, set_name, set_type, rulings_uri, rarity, artist, artist_ids, edhrec_rank, penny_rank, prices, purchase_uris, scryfall_uri, scryfall_set_uri, collector_number, content_warning, set_uri, illustration_id 2. Discarded Card Attributes: uri, layout, highres_image, image_status, games, reserved, finishes, oversized, promo, reprint, variation, prints_search_uri, digital, card_back_id, attraction_lights, flavor_text, flavor_uris, flavor_name, border_color, frame, frame_effects, full_art, textless, booster, story_spotlight, related_uris

docs.title: Edge Case Handling
docs.text:
• Card Not Found: If a card is not found, the API returns a 404 Not Found status.
  • Rate Limit Exceeded: If the rate limit is exceeded, the API returns a 429 Too Many Requests status.
  • Invalid Parameters: If invalid parameters are provided, the API returns a 400 Bad Request status.

docs.title: Purpose & Scope
docs.text:
This document describes the system architecture, design, decisions, components, data model, security requirements, deployment topology, operation requirements, and integration of the Arcane Archive backend. Arcane Archive is a Magic: The Gathering companion application with a React Native, Expo, TypeScript, with a FastAPI REST API.

The backend supports the following features:

  1. Public card and set data retrieval.
  2. User authentication and authorization.
  3. User profile management.
  4. Card library management.
  5. Wishlist management.
  6. Deck building and management.
  7. Game tracking.
  8. Integration with Scryfall API for card data and images.
  9. Mobile-friendly design.
  10. AI-assisted deck building (planned for future implementation).

See Overview & Installation for more information on how to install and run the backend.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Feature Scope FastAPI Backend HTTP routers, pydantic schemas, database models Local user authentication JWT-based authentication with password hashing and salting Firebase social authentication OAuth2-based authentication with Google, Facebook, and Apple Simple & Advanced Search Search for cards by name, set, or other criteria Scryfall API Integration Bulk downloads, normalization, and database upserts Player Profile Management User profile management, preferences, and game stats Card Library Management Manage card collections, wishlists, and sets Wishlist Management Create, edit, and delete wishlists Deck Builder Create, edit, and manage decks Card Scanner Scan cards to add to the user's library Redis Caching Cache-aside for public card data pgVector & AI Deck Builder (Future) Store AI-generated card embeddings for semantic search pgBouncer & pgBackRest Connection pooling and backup/recovery for PostgreSQL

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: Arcane Archive is designed to be maintainable, scalable, testable, and reliable. Its backend architecture combines SOLID principles, a layered architecture, the repository pattern, transaction management, the adaptor pattern, and dependency injection within a modular monolith.

docs.title: Architectural Layers
docs.text:
1. Presentation Layer: FastAPI routers, Pydantic, Request/Response schemas
  2. Application Layer: Register user, save deck, search cards
  3. Domain Layer: Card quantity, deck format, ownership rules
  4. Data Access Layer: User, credentials, card, and deck repositories
  5. Infrastructure Layer: SQLAlchemy, Redis, Firebase Admin SDK, Scryfall API, pgBouncer, pgBackRest

docs.title: SOLID Principles
docs.text:
• Single Responsibility Principle – Each file has one job (e.g., user_repository only talks to the database).
  • Open/Closed Principle – The application is open for extension but closed for modification allowing for future enhancements like adding an AI Deck Service.
  • Liskov Substitution Principle – Example: Different auth methods (local and Firebase social auth) can both be used interchangeably with the token schema without affecting the application's behavior.
  • Interface Segregation Principle – Instead of one giant repository, I have separated the repositories into smaller, more focused components to only pull in the data they need.
  • Dependency Inversion Principle – Services don't create their own database connections but instead ask for them through the dependencies they need.

docs.title: Architectural Styles & Design Patterns
docs.text:
Category Selected Pattern Architectural Style Modular Monolith Architectural Pattern Layered Architecture Design Principle Separation of Concerns Persistence Pattern Repository Pattern & Transaction Management Composition Pattern Dependency Injection Integration Pattern Adapter Pattern Caching Pattern Cache-Aside Data Processing Pattern ETL Pipeline (Extract, Transform, Load) Resilience Approach Graceful Degradation

See References for more information on the design patterns I used in this project.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
Microservices Architecture

I considered using a microservices architecture for this project, but I decided against it for several reasons:

  • Complexity: A microservices architecture would add complexity to the application. I found that a modular monolith is simpler to develop, test, and deploy, debug, and maintain. It also allows me to focus on the core functionality of the application while maintaining separation of concerns.
  • Performance: With microservices latency and network communication could potentially introduce performance issues. A modular monolith fits better for Arcane Archive's current requirements, as it eliminates network overhead and allows for faster communication between components.
  • Deployment: Using a modular monolith allows me to deploy the application as a single unit, which is simpler and easier to manage.
  • Scalability: Microservices can provide better scalability, but I found that a modular monolith can still be scaled horizontally by adding more instances of the application. This is enough to satisfy the current requirements of Arcane Archive. If the application grows in complexity and requires more scalability, I can refactor the application into a microservices architecture in the future.

Decision: I selected a modular monolith because it fits best with the current project requirements, while still allowing me to scale the application in the future if needed. It also provides a balanced approach for maintainability, testability, and performance.

Routes accessing the database directly

I considered having the API routes access the database directly, but I decided against it for several reasons:

  • Separation of Concerns: By having the API routes access the database directly, I would be mixing concerns between the API layer and the data access layer. This would make the code harder to maintain and test.
  • Testability: By having the API routes access the database directly, it would be harder to test the application. By using a service layer, I can easily mock the service layer for testing without needing to access the database.
  • Flexibility: By having the API routes access the database directly, I would be tightly coupling the API layer to the data access layer. This would make it harder to change the data access layer in the future without affecting the API layer. By using a service layer, I can easily change the data access layer without affecting the API layer.
  • Reusability: By having the API routes access the database directly, I would be duplicating code across multiple routes. By using a service layer, I can reuse the same service methods across multiple routes, reducing code duplication and improving maintainability.
  • Security: By having the API routes access the database directly, I would be exposing the database to potential security vulnerabilities. By using a service layer, I can implement security measures such as input validation and authentication in a centralized location, reducing the risk of security vulnerabilities.
  • Maintainability: By having the API routes access the database directly, I would be making the code harder to maintain.

Decision: I selected a layered architecture with application services because it provides a clean separation of concerns between the API layer and the data access layer, while still allowing me to easily test, maintain, scale, and secure the application. It also allows me to reuse code across multiple routes, reducing code duplication and improving maintainability.

docs.title: Ownership & Responsibility
docs.text:
1. Scryfall & Wizards of the Coast own the card data and images. Arcane Archive stores the data in a PostgreSQL database.
  2. Arcane Archive owns the user data and authentication as well as accounts, collections, wishlists, saved decks, and game stats.
  3. PostgreSQL is the normal local read source.
  4. Wizards of the Coast own the artwork and MTG intellectual property.
  5. Users own their personal data and are responsible for managing their account information and privacy settings.
  6. Redis is a non-authoritative cache and entries may expire.

docs.title: Domain Model & Database Design
docs.text: The following ERD shows the database design for the Arcane Archive backend.

docs.title: Card ID and Deck Validation
docs.text: Scryfall identifies cards by their unique Scryfall ID. An Oracle ID is a unique identifier for a card that is used to group all printings of a card together. A card can have multiple printings, and each printing can have a different edition, language, finish, or condition, etc.

docs.title: Card Data Ingestion
docs.text:
The target for Arcane Archive is to ingest Scryfall's bulk data file containing 52,000+ cards. This will allow me to have a high-performance application that will remain sustainable at zero cost. A daily import of the bulk data file will take place to provide the most up-to-date card data.

Card Ingestion Process: 1. Retrieve and Download the bulk data file from Scryfall's API. 2. Validate and normalize the data while preserving Scryfall's identifiers. 3. Upsert the data into the PostgreSQL database, ensuring that existing records are updated and new records are inserted. 4. Publish the updated card data to the Redis cache for real-time updates. 5. Record the latest version, import time, record counts, duration, rejected records, and outcome. 6. Retain the last successful catalog on download, validation, or import failure and alert on staleness.

See Scryfall Bulk Data and API Usage Guide for more information on the bulk data file format.

docs.title: Local-First Card Retrieval & Failure Handling
docs.text:
Card search uses Redis as a cache-aside for public card data. The application will first attempt to retrieve the catalog from Redis. If the Redis cache is unavailable, the application will attempt to retrieve the catalog from the local catalog. If the local catalog is unavailable, the application will attempt to retrieve the catalog from Scryfall's API.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Router
    participant Service as Card Search Service
    participant Data as Card Retrieval Adapter
    participant Cache as Redis
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant External as Scryfall API
    Client->>Router: GET /cards/search
    Router->>Service: Search with validated parameters
    Service->>Data: Retrieve normalized card results
    Data->>Cache: Read public query cache
    alt Valid cache hit
        Cache-->>Data: Cached results
    else Miss or cache unavailable
        Data->>DB: Query local catalog
        alt Local query succeeds
            DB-->>Data: Results (possibly empty)
            opt Cache available
                Data->>Cache: Store results with TTL
            end
        else Local catalog unavailable
            opt Approved external fallback for this query
                Data->>External: Bounded HTTPS lookup
                External-->>Data: Result or upstream error
            end
        end
    end
    Data-->>Service: Normalized result or availability error
    Service-->>Router: Use case result
    Router-->>Client: HTTP response

docs.title: User Registration Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Router
    participant Auth as Authentication Service
    participant Users as User Repository
    participant Creds as Credential Repository
    participant UOW as Transaction Boundary
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    Client->>Router: POST /register
    Router->>Auth: Register validated input
    Auth->>Auth: Check policy and hash password
    Auth->>UOW: Begin transaction
    Auth->>Users: Check account identifiers
    Users->>DB: Query existing user
    alt Account conflict
        Auth->>UOW: Roll back
        Auth-->>Router: Registration conflict
        Router-->>Client: Conflict response
    else No existing account
        Auth->>Users: Create user and flush
        Users->>DB: INSERT user
        Auth->>Creds: Create local credential
        Creds->>DB: INSERT credential
        alt Writes and commit succeed
            Auth->>UOW: Commit
            Auth-->>Router: Registration result
            Router-->>Client: 201 Created
        else Constraint or persistence failure
            Auth->>UOW: Roll back
            Auth-->>Router: Mapped error
            Router-->>Client: Appropriate error response
        end
    end

docs.title: Cloud Infrastructure Selection
docs.text: I selected Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) for this project primarily due to its always free tier which allows for cost efficiency without sacrificing performance. Their Ampere A1 compute shapes provide a high memory capacity of 24GBs, which is required to host the application, a PostgreSQL database, and a Redis Cache in a single instance. The free tier will also be enough for the data ingestion of Scryfall's bulk data file containing 52,000+ cards. This allows me to have a high-performance application that will remain sustainable at zero cost.

docs.title: DMZ & Network Architecture
docs.text:
I implemented a DMZ(Demilitarized Zone) to separate the public-facing services from the internal services. This provides an additional layer of security and helps to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data like user credentials. I did this using OCI's Virtual Cloud Network (VCN). By placing the API and Database in a private subnet and only exposing the load balancer to the public, I ensure that user data remains unaccessible from the public internet.

I implemented several security measures to protect user data and ensure the integrity of the application. These include using HTTPS for all API requests and implementing JWT authentication for secure user sessions. Additionally, I use dependency injection for testability and loose coupling, which helps to prevent injection attacks.

I used NGINX as a reverse proxy to handle the incoming requests. This is the entry point within the DMZ which ensures that all incoming requests are authenticated and encrypted before reaching the API.

I used the OCI Service Gateway to ensure that the API can securely communicate with OCI Object Storage for card image storage and retrieval. This allows the private subnet to securely access OCI Object Storage without exposing it to the public internet.

I used OCI Logging and Monitoring to ensure that the application is monitored and that any errors are detected and addressed as soon as possible. This also provides me with visibility of the Docker stack to manage the 24GBs of RAM for the Oracle Cloud infrastructure efficiently.

docs.title: SQL Vs. NoSQL Database
docs.text: I chose to use a PostgreSQL Database for this project because it provides a robust and reliable way to store and retrieve data. PostgreSQL is well-suited for complex queries and transactions, which are essential for handling user collections, wishlists, and other features of the Arcane Archive application. Additionally, PostgreSQL provides ACID compliance, which ensures data consistency and reliability. By choosing PostgreSQL, I also gain access to the pgvector extension. This will allow me to store AI-generated card embeddings for semantic search, which enables the AI Deck Builder to find cards based on their 'feel' or 'strategy' rather than just keywords.

docs.title: PostgreSQL with pgVector
docs.text: I chose PostgreSQL for its ACID compliance and robustness in handling complex queries for user collections. By using pgVector, I can store AI-generated card embeddings. This enables a semantic search feature allowing the AI Deck Builder to find cards based on strategic feel, like aggressive, defensive, or control, rather than just keyword matching.

docs.title: Dual-Path Data Ingestion with Scryfall API & Bulk Data File
docs.text: I chose to use Scryfall's API for real-time card data updates and to adhere to their API usage policies. However, for bulk data ingestion, I use Scryfall's bulk data file to ensure data consistency and to avoid hitting the API rate limit. This approach allows for a balance between real-time updates and efficient data ingestion.

docs.title: Scryfall Data Usage and Rate Limiting
docs.text: To adhere to Scryfall's API usage policies, I implemented a 100ms rate limit for all calls to api.scryfall.com to avoid 429 errors. For image assets, I used a Bulk-to-CDN path: the app extracts image URIs from the locally processed bulk JSON file and fetches the assets from the .scryfall.io domain. Because the image CDN is decoupled from the primary API rate limits (scryfall.io doesn't require a rate limit), this allows the app to lazily cache high-resolution card art to OCI Object Storage without risking an API ban.

docs.title: Hotlinking Vs. Object Storage
docs.text:
To avoid hotlinking issues, I chose to use OCI Object Storage to store card images. Images that are not used are not directly linked from Scryfall's servers, reducing the risk of being blocked by Scryfall's rate limits or \ other policies.

Because the image CDN is decoupled from the primary API rate limits on Scryfall's API (scryfall.io doesn't require a rate limit), this allows the app to lazily cache high-resolution card art to OCI Object Storage without risking an API ban.

I will implement this lazy loading strategy where the application first checks the OCI Object Storage for the card image, and if the card is not found, it fetches the card image from Scryfall's CDN. This ensures that the application does not exceed the rate limit on api.scryfall.com and minimizes API calls.

docs.title: AsyncSession for Database Transactions
docs.text: I chose to use AsyncSession for database transactions because it allows multiple concurrent database transactions without blocking other transactions, improving performance and scalability.

docs.title: Dependency Injection for Testability
docs.text: I chose to use FastAPI's Dependency Injection for testability. This allows for easy mocking of repositories during testing, which high code coverage without needing a live database connection. Dependency Injection also provides loose coupling and makes the codebase more testable, maintainable, and scalable.

docs.title: Connection Pooling with pgBouncer
docs.text:
I chose to use pgBouncer for connection pooling, a cache of database connections that can be reused for multiple client requests to improve performance and reduce the number of database connections. This also helps to prevent connection overload and ensures efficient resource utilization. This would allow hundreds of concurrent mobile sessions with only a small number of database connections.*

This will significantly reduce the overhead on the 24GBs RAM allowance with Oracle Cloud and prevents "too many connections" errors, which are commonly encountered with high-traffic MTG searches.

docs.title: In-memory Caching with Redis
docs.text: I chose to use Redis for in-memory caching to reduce latency and improve performance for frequently accessed data like search results and card data.*

docs.title: Data Backup and Recovery with pgBackRest
docs.text: I chose to use pgBackRest for data backup and recovery. This ensures that data is backed up regularly and can be restored in case of a disaster or data loss. pgBackRest provides Point-in-Time Recovery, allowing me to recover the database to a specific second if a data corruption event occurs.

docs.title: CAP: Consistency & Partition Tolerance
docs.text: I chose to prioritize Consistency and Partition Tolerance for this project. This is because the Arcane Archive application requires data consistency and reliability for user collections, wishlists, and other features. Consistency ensures that data is accurate and up to date, while Partition Tolerance allows the application to continue functioning even if some parts of the system fail. Users expect their data to be accurate and reliable, and this approach ensures that the application meets those expectations. A user would rather hit retry than see incorrect or incomplete data (e.g., missing cards in their collection or incomplete deck creation).

docs.title: Data Integrity via Schemas
docs.text: I chose to use Pydantic schemas for data validation and normalization. This ensures that data is consistent and reliable and helps to prevent errors and inconsistencies in the database. This also ensures that sensitive database information is protected and is never exposed to the outside world.

docs.title: Dependency Management and Virtual Environment
docs.text: I decided to use Poetry for dependency management and virtual environment management mainly for its ease of use and flexibility. By using Poetry, I can easily manage dependencies and virtual environments for my project, ensuring a consistent and reproducible development environment. Using Poetry's lockfile also ensures deterministic builds, allowing for consistent and reliable dependencies across different environments (e.g., development, testing, and production). This effectively eliminates "It works on my machine" bugs.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
To ensure the Arcane Archive backend can handle an increased load and traffic, the following scalability strategies are applied:

  1. In-memory caching with Redis for caching search results and card data to reduce latency and improve performance.
  2. Load balancing to distribute incoming traffic across multiple server instances.
  3. Database optimization with indexing and read replicas to enhance query performance and handle an increased load.
  4. Asynchronous task processing with Celery and RabbitMQ for handling background tasks like card data updates.
  5. Containerization with Docker for consistent deployment across different environments.
  6. Horizontal scaling by adding more instances of the application server as demand increases.

docs.title: Dependency Injection
docs.text:
I designed Arcane Archive to be flexible and modular by using dependency injection. This allows me to replace real dependencies with mocks during testing and makes the code more testable, maintainable, and scalable. The following diagram illustrates the dependency injection flow for a request:
